overview: This file brings together U.S. diplomatic reporting, Chinese and Formosan nationalist propaganda, State Department memoranda, cross-reference sheets, and later wartime planning documents concerning Taiwan’s political future. Its central theme is the campaign by Chinese authorities and the Formosan Revolutionary League to secure Taiwan’s return to China after Japan’s defeat, partly in response to discussion of Korean independence, international trusteeship, and possible Taiwanese independence or autonomy. The documents also assess the revolutionary movement’s history, organization, intelligence and terrorist activities, political reliability, Kuomintang connections, and requests for American aid, while later papers address Chinese preparations for administering Taiwan and U.S. policy on military government. Although the file title covers February–April 1942, the bundle includes related documents and cross-references extending through October 1944.

subfiles.title: State Department summary of Chungking despatch no. 342
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the embassy’s reporting on China’s sudden wartime interest in Taiwan’s postwar disposition.
subfiles.summary: Memo notes few Formosans in unoccupied China, their use of Japanese extraterritorial protection in Fujian, and dates China's publicity campaign to forestall Taiwanese independence proposals to the Pacific War's outbreak.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 342: Chinese Publicity Regarding the Formosan Question
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, U.S. Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Reports and evaluates Chinese publicity calling for Taiwan’s postwar reunion with China.
subfiles.summary: Gauss relays propaganda and Sun Fo's claim Taiwan would return to China, judging the Formosan movement weak and questioning delegate authenticity, arguing China exploited the changed war situation and racial ties to forestall Taiwanese independence proposals.

subfiles.title: Inauguration Manifesto of the Formosan Revolutionary Federation
subfiles.to: Formosans, mainland Chinese, and international supporters
subfiles.about: Proclaims the federation’s formation and calls for unified resistance to Japanese rule under the Chinese national flag.
subfiles.summary: Manifesto claims Taiwan as historically Chinese, lost via the Shimonoseki treaty, citing Taiwanese resistance and wartime participation; the federation pledges to overthrow Japanese rule, restore Taiwan, and ally with other oppressed peoples.

subfiles.title: Outlines of Policy of the Formosan Revolutionary Federation
subfiles.about: Defines the federation’s program of recovering Taiwan through participation in China’s anti-Japanese war.
subfiles.summary: Statement declares Taiwan's revolution part of China's, accepting the Three People's Principles and Chiang's leadership, calling to overthrow Japan and unify Formosans with Korean and Japanese resistance.

subfiles.title: Formosa Revolutionaries Hold Conference Here
subfiles.about: Reports a Chungking conference seeking armed restoration of Taiwan as a Chinese province.
subfiles.summary: Report says over thirty representatives adopted resolutions for underground work, armed forces, and restoring Taiwan to China, naming League officers elected.

subfiles.title: Formosans Seeking Reunion with China
subfiles.about: Advocates Taiwan’s reunion with China and offers a propagandistic history of resistance to Japanese rule.
subfiles.summary: Article distinguishes Taiwanese reunion demands from Korean independence demands, argues China's war declaration voided the Shimonoseki treaty, cites Taiwan's strategic value and alleged unrest, and profiles Li Youbang and Formosan revolutionary groups proposing a restoration army.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on Taiwan’s history and administration
subfiles.from: Department of State, Far Eastern Affairs (Hornbeck)
subfiles.about: Points to a two-part memorandum on Taiwan’s history, Japanese administration, and popular attitudes.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a memorandum on Taiwan's history and Japanese administrative practice/population attitudes, filed under 894A.014/2.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hull memorandum on Taiwan’s possible return to China
subfiles.about: References a postwar-planning memorandum about the possibility of returning Taiwan to China.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a Hull memorandum on Taiwan's possible restoration to China, filed under 840.50/2088.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 1484 on the Formosan Revolutionists League
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., U.S. Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Chungking
subfiles.about: Transmits an embassy assessment of the Formosan Revolutionists League’s strength, aims, activities, and Chinese connections.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson reports the Formosan Revolutionists League claimed 140,000 members, though only about 1,000 were actually in unoccupied China, aiming at a Formosan army and restoration to China via propaganda and espionage.

subfiles.title: Edward E. Rice memorandum on the Formosan Revolutionists League
subfiles.from: Edward E. Rice, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.to: American Embassy and Department of State
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed history, organizational chart, operational assessment, and evaluation of the Formosan Revolutionists League.
subfiles.summary: Rice traces Taiwanese revolutionary societies from the Taiwan Reform Society through the creation of the League in 1941 and describes its six constituent organizations and principal officials. He details its claimed territorial divisions, membership, propaganda, espionage, terrorist activity, Kuomintang relationship, and offer to conduct intelligence and naval-piloting work for the United States. The memorandum is deeply skeptical of its inflated membership claims, internal unity, intelligence reliability, and several leaders’ loyalties, though it considers Chang Pang-chieh genuinely anti-Japanese. It concludes that the League had little immediate influence but might become important when Japanese control weakened.

subfiles.title: Declaration on the forty-eighth anniversary of Taiwan’s cession
subfiles.to: Taiwanese people, China, and the Allied nations
subfiles.about: Rejects an international mandate and demands Taiwan’s restoration to China under Atlantic Charter principles.
subfiles.summary: Declaration portrays Taiwan's people as Chinese victims of 48 years of Japanese rule, asks Allies to support restoration to China, condemns international-mandate proposals as against the Atlantic Charter, and urges resistance and a Free China provincial government.

subfiles.title: Broadcast of Secretary General Wu Tieh-chen
subfiles.about: Affirms the Kuomintang’s responsibility and national policy to recover Taiwan from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wu calls Taiwan's cession a national shame, urging Formosans to hasten Japan's defeat, invoking Sun Yat-sen and Chiang's 1938 pledge to free Korea and Taiwan toward restoration.

subfiles.title: Rothwell memorandum on redrafted military-government letters
subfiles.about: Forwards revised covering letters for approved State Department papers on military government in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Rothwell says he redrafted letters stating Taiwan military-government papers have formal approval but remain open to revision, asking Ballantine to secure Grew's and the Secretary's approval.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Taiwan military-government papers to General Hilldring
subfiles.about: Transmits the State Department’s formally approved views on political and policy questions concerning military government in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Dunn sends copies of 'Military Government in Formosa' to General Hilldring, noting the papers now represent current State policy, subject to later modification.

subfiles.title: Letter transmitting Taiwan military-government papers to Captain Pence
subfiles.about: Sends the Navy formally approved State Department papers on military government in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: Dunn sends the same Taiwan military-government papers to Captain Pence, stating they now express approved State Department views subject to revision.

subfiles.title: Despatch on formation of the Formosa Problems Investigation Committee
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, U.S. Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese establishment of a committee to study Taiwan and evaluates competing expectations about the island’s political future.
subfiles.summary: Gauss reports China's eleven-member Formosa Problems Investigation Committee under Chen Yi, seen as a belated response to approaching American forces; he stresses Chinese ignorance of the island and notes many literate Taiwanese fear mainland rule, preferring independence or autonomy.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs transmittal note for a two-part Taiwan memorandum
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Introduces a two-section study of Taiwan’s history, Japanese administration, and the attitudes of its inhabitants.
subfiles.summary: Note states Langdon wrote the historical first section and Emmerson the second, on Japanese administration and Taiwanese attitudes, of a two-part Taiwan study.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum proposing additions to a Taiwan study
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Recommends expanding a Taiwan paper with historical sections on the island, American and Chinese interests, and Japan’s acquisition of it.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck calls the existing Taiwan paper good but incomplete, proposing added general and U.S./China history sections and Pasvolsky's addition to distribution.

interest: Shows wartime contest between Taiwanese restoration-to-China claims and skeptical U.S. intelligence on factional, inflated movements.
